title: Omar Abdullah Fact-Checks JP Nadda Over JKSSB Paper Leak Timeline
excerpt: The J&K Chief Minister corrected the BJP leader's claim about the JKSSB paper leak date, pointing out it occurred under LG administration — not his government — as the NEET controversy roils Parliament.
body:
• J&K Chief Minister Omar Abdullah corrected BJP leader JP Nadda's claim about the JKSSB paper leak, pointing out the date error in Nadda's statement
  • The exchange came as Nadda attempted to deflect from the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak controversy by citing alleged paper leaks in opposition-governed states
  • The JKSSB sub-inspector recruitment exam paper leak of 2022 occurred when J&K was under Lt. Governor administration, not under Abdullah's elected government
  • The Opposition accused the BJP of a "deliberate attempt to deceive people" by conflating timelines of paper leak incidents across states

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah publicly corrected Union Minister JP Nadda over factual inaccuracies about the JKSSB paper leak, accusing the BJP leader of getting the date wrong in an apparent attempt to shift blame during the ongoing NEET paper leak crisis.

The Factual Dispute

The confrontation arose after Nadda, at a press conference during the Parliament Monsoon Session, accused opposition-governed states of presiding over paper leak scandals, including an alleged JKSSB recruitment exam paper leak in Jammu and Kashmir. The claim was part of the BJP's strategy to deflect mounting pressure over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak, which has triggered student protests, opposition demands for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation, and repeated disruptions in Parliament.

Abdullah responded sharply, pointing out that Nadda had confused the timeline. The JKSSB sub-inspector recruitment exam paper leak occurred in 2022, when Jammu and Kashmir was governed not by Abdullah's National Conference but by the centrally appointed Lt. Governor administration — a period when the BJP-led central government had direct control over the union territory's affairs.

"You got the date wrong."

— Omar Abdullah, Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir, addressing JP Nadda's claims

BJP's Deflection Strategy

Nadda's press conference was part of a broader BJP effort to counter the opposition's offensive on the NEET paper leak. The Union Minister questioned Congress leader Rahul Gandhi for being "selective" about paper leak incidents, accusing him of ignoring alleged irregularities in states governed by INDIA alliance parties, including Telangana, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Karnataka.

The BJP argued that paper leaks were not limited to one party or state, urging the Opposition to discuss irregularities wherever they occurred rather than "politicising" the issue. Nadda called for a collaborative approach to finding solutions.

Opposition Hits Back

The Opposition, however, slammed the BJP's approach as a "deliberate attempt to deceive people." Multiple INDIA alliance parties accused the ruling party of fabricating or misrepresenting "Congress-era paper leak claims" to distract from the NEET scandal, which led to the cancellation of the NEET-UG 2026 exam in May after allegations of paper leaks surfaced.

BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari responded to Abdullah's fact-check, accusing the J&K Chief Minister of lying. The exchange underscored the deepening political divide over examination integrity, with both sides trading accusations of dishonesty.

The Broader Paper Leak Crisis

The Abdullah-Nadda exchange is a sideshow in the larger NEET paper leak crisis that has consumed Parliament's Monsoon Session. Congress leader Jairam Ramesh warned that the session risks becoming a "washout" unless the government agrees to a discussion on the NEET scandal. Opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were detained by Delhi Police during a protest march near the Prime Minister's residence.

For the Indian diaspora, the recurring paper leak scandals raise fundamental questions about the integrity of India's examination system. Over the past seven years, more than 60 paper leak incidents have been documented across various national and state-level examinations, affecting millions of aspirants and eroding confidence in competitive exams that remain a primary pathway to social mobility.

What's Next

With Parliament sessions continuing to be disrupted, the government has indicated readiness for a discussion on NEET but has resisted opposition demands for the Education Minister's resignation as a precondition. Prime Minister Narendra Modi recently announced the creation of fast-track courts for paper leak cases, signalling an acknowledgement of the scale of the problem even as the political blame game intensifies.
